sections.skill: Plan charitable giving, research charities, and understand the tax treatment of donations

questions.prompt: Nia wants to give 5% of her $2,400 monthly take-home pay to charity. How much is that each month?
questions.intro: Many people plan giving as part of their budget, often as a percent of income. Giving time (volunteering) and skills also counts.
sources: IRS (Tax Exempt Organization Search): Lists organizations eligible to receive tax-deductible charitable contributions. (https://apps.irs.gov/app/eos/)

IRS (Charitable contribution deductions): Charitable contributions are deductible only to qualified organizations; itemizers deduct them on Schedule A. (https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits/charitable-organizations/charitable-contribution-deductions)

New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs (Charities Registration): Most charities that solicit in New Jersey must register with the state, and residents can look up registration status. (https://www.njconsumeraffairs.gov/charities/)

FTC (How to donate wisely and avoid charity scams): Research charities before giving, be wary of pressure and payment by gift card or wire, and watch for scams after disasters. (https://consumer.ftc.gov/features/how-donate-wisely-and-avoid-charity-scams)

IRS (Working Families Tax Cuts): Beginning in tax year 2026, taxpayers who do not itemize can deduct up to $1,000 ($2,000 married filing jointly) of eligible cash gifts to qualified charities. (https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/working-families-tax-cuts)

questions.prompt: For tax year 2026, Nia files single and takes the standard deduction. She gave $1,440 in cash to qualified charities. Using the 2026 rule for people who do not itemize, how much can she deduct for those gifts?
questions.intro: Starting with tax year 2026, people who take the standard deduction can also deduct cash gifts to qualified charities: up to $1,000 for single filers or $2,000 for married couples filing jointly. Itemizers deduct gifts under the itemized rules instead. A deduction lowers taxable income; it is not a dollar-for-dollar refund.
questions.feedback: Her $1,440 is above the $1,000 single cap, so $1,000 is deductible.

misconceptions.A: Uses the rule from before 2026, when non-itemizers got no charitable deduction
